clue.text: Give something temporarily, in the spot where you hit the hay–some like their liquor this way.

definitions.text: some like their liquor this way
definitions.note: describes the answer as an adjective: whisky mixed from several malts

indicators.note: in the spot means the lending word sits inside the bed word

parts.words: the spot where you hit the hay
parts.note: to hit the hay is to go to bed, so the spot is a bed
to give something temporarily is to lend it

explanation.surface: A host lends a guest a bed and pours whisky the way some drinkers prefer it.
explanation.definitionFit: Blended whisky is a mix of malts and grains, a style many drinkers prefer to single malt.

clue.text: One version of a large printed handkerchief, with the second letter as well as a first one coming from it.

definitions.text: One version of a large printed handkerchief, with the second letter as well as a first one coming from it.

parts.words: One version of a large printed handkerchief, with the second letter as well as a first one coming from it.
parts.note: one spelling of the patterned neckerchief; it opens with B and A, the alphabet's second and first letters

explanation.walkthrough: The word is spelt with a double or a single N; this is the shorter version, and its first two letters are B and A.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandana is a large brightly patterned handkerchief worn around the neck or head.

clue.text: Supposedly you have this condition when someone is talking about you–being within listening range.

definitions.text: Supposedly you have this condition when someone is talking about you
definitions.meaning: folklore says your ears burn when others gossip about you
the distance within which a sound can be heard

explanation.walkthrough: Split the word as EARS HOT for the first sense; whole, it is the range of hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Earshot is the distance over which a voice can be heard, as in within earshot.

clue.text: Falls down because of certain medication.

definitions.meaning: medicine given by the drop, as for eyes or ears

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a fall caused by drugs; the two halves are separate senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for falling and a noun for liquid medicine dispensed in small droplets.

clue.text: Sid and I worry with it, causing scorn, possibly.

definitions.note: possibly flags that scorn is one way of putting it

indicators.note: to worry something is to shake it about, as a dog worries a bone, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: Sid and the speaker fret over it until it breeds contempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Disdain is contempt or scorn, the feeling that someone is unworthy of respect.

clue.text: It comes after the meal, with the lead in what the cow chews.

indicators.note: with the lead in tells us the star goes inside the cow's chew

parts.note: a cow chews its cud
the lead in a play or film is its star

explanation.surface: A farmyard picture: something follows a meal while the cow keeps chewing.
explanation.definitionFit: Custard is a pudding, so it is served as dessert once the main course is over.

clue.text: A cheesy place, by all accounts! Just gorge there!

definitions.text: A cheesy place, by all accounts! Just gorge there!

parts.words: A cheesy place, by all accounts! Just gorge there!
parts.note: a village famous for its cheese, which also has a famous gorge; gorge also means stuff yourself

explanation.walkthrough: Cheddar is a village in Somerset, England, that gave its name to the cheese, and Cheddar Gorge is a limestone ravine beside it; 'gorge' also invites you to feast.
explanation.definitionFit: The Somerset village is the original home of cheddar cheese and sits at the foot of Cheddar Gorge.

clue.text: The colonies didn't like its passage–but it's a way of putting your foot down!

definitions.text: The colonies didn't like its passage
definitions.meaning: the 1765 British tax on printed papers that angered the American colonies

definitions.text: a way of putting your foot down

explanation.walkthrough: The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed printed matter in Britain's American colonies; 'passage' is the passing of a law.
explanation.definitionFit: The law's name doubles as a description of the physical act of stamping down hard.

clue.text: Forever being such–let mail get delivered from it.

indicators.note: mail that gets delivered from it is let out of its order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A forever stamp, let your mail go out from it.
explanation.definitionFit: All-time describes something unsurpassed for ever, as in an all-time record.

clue.text: Quits what may be side streets shortly.

indicators.note: what may be signals that the letters can be made into another word

parts.note: STS is the short form of streets

explanation.surface: Someone gives up on what might be the back streets.
explanation.definitionFit: To desist is to cease or stop doing something, so it is a synonym of quits.

clue.text: What comes from the bow, in opposite points, gets thinner and thinner.

indicators.note: in opposite points places the arrow between the two compass letters

parts.note: north and south are opposite points of the compass
an archer's bow shoots an arrow

explanation.surface: An archer's shot seems to taper as it flies off in opposite directions.
explanation.definitionFit: A river or road that narrows becomes less wide, tapering progressively.

clue.text: Makes things possible with bean soup to the French.

indicators.note: turning beans into soup mashes them up, so their letters are mixed

parts.note: les is the French plural word for the

explanation.surface: Bean soup served to the French is what allows things to happen.
explanation.definitionFit: To enable is to make possible, so the answer is a synonym of the whole phrase.

clue.text: Well, you wouldn't feel them, most likely!

definitions.text: Well, you wouldn't feel them, most likely!

parts.words: Well, you wouldn't feel them, most likely!
parts.note: reads as a shrug, but well is the adjective healthy: a healthy person feels no minor ailments

explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' looks like an interjection opening the sentence; it means in good health.
explanation.definitionFit: Aches and pains are the minor bodily complaints of illness or age, which a healthy person would not suffer.

clue.text: See 11
See 11
Part of play to a long, long time, being a hunter who peeked at the dipper.

definitions.text: a hunter who peeked at the dipper

parts.note: a play is divided into acts
an aeon is an immensely long age

explanation.surface: A stage act meets an endless age and a hunter spying on a bather.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth the hunter Actaeon saw the goddess Artemis bathing; she turned him into a stag. The dipper here is a bather, not a ladle or a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Actaeon is the mythological hunter punished for glimpsing the goddess while she bathed.

clue.text: A short dash–500–has to be the last part.

parts.note: an en dash is the shorter typographic dash
D is the Roman numeral for 500

explanation.surface: A quick sprint of 500 metres must be the final stage of a race.
explanation.definitionFit: The end is the final portion of anything, its concluding section.

clue.text: Those first-level books you may have had kicked Ed's rear!

indicators.note: a kicked rear is knocked about, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: The schoolbooks of your early years might have been used to kick Ed's backside.
explanation.definitionFit: Readers are graded books for children learning to read, the first level of schoolbooks.

clue.text: See 6
If you get into hot water, you may be!

definitions.text: If you get into hot water, you may be!

parts.words: If you get into hot water, you may be!
parts.note: hot water is the idiom for trouble, but taken literally a dip in it burns you

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot water' reads as the idiom for trouble; taken literally, it burns the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: To be scalded is to be burnt by hot liquid or steam, which is what very hot water does.

clue.text: You and I come up on a bad mark–keep things that way!

indicators.note: in a down clue on places the first part above the second
in a down clue coming up means reading from the bottom upward

parts.note: together you and I are us
a stain is a blot or blemish

explanation.surface: Two people rise above a blemish and resolve to keep the status quo.
explanation.definitionFit: To sustain something is to maintain it as it is, keeping it going without change.

clue.text: An old horse and the head of the flock, with the shore taken as an example of the third word here.

definitions.text: the shore taken as an example of the third word here
definitions.note: the third word of the clue is horse, and shore rearranges its letters

parts.note: an is the indefinite article a
a nag is a worn-out horse
a ram is the male that leads a flock of sheep

explanation.surface: An aged horse and a lead ram stand beside the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points back at the clue itself: SHORE is a rearrangement of HORSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A word formed by rearranging another word's letters is the device this term names.

clue.text: Supposedly ties pay them, even though they are bad leaders.

indicators.note: bad leaders are disordered ones, so the letters of leaders are scrambled

explanation.surface: A warning that some officials get paid off even though they lead badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' rearranges LEADERS. In blackjack a tie is often said to go to the dealer, the house's player.
explanation.definitionFit: Casino dealers represent the house, which by popular belief wins tied hands.

clue.text: With a knotted tie, clad in this–which might be your strong point!

definitions.text: which might be your strong point

indicators.note: a knotted tie is twisted up, so the letters of tie and clad are tangled together

explanation.surface: Dressed in a well-knotted tie, a person shows off their best quality.
explanation.definitionFit: A citadel is a fortress, a strong point in the military sense rather than a talent.

clue.text: Here in Montreal in crazy cold, found at the end of one's will?

definitions.text: found at the end of one's will

indicators.note: in crazy cold places the French word inside the mixed-up letters
crazy cold means the letters of cold are jumbled

parts.note: ici is French for here, and Montreal is French-speaking

explanation.surface: Someone in a freezing Montreal winter adds a last note to their will.
explanation.definitionFit: A codicil is a supplement added to a will, usually appended at its end.

clue.text: See 24 across
Heard about the old king and Edward sometimes, if schooled this way?

parts.note: Lear is Shakespeare's ancient king
and is sometimes shortened to 'n', as in rock 'n' roll
Ed is the short form of Edward

explanation.surface: Learning about King Lear and Edward is what education teaches.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'sometimes' warns that 'and' is shortened to 'n'; 'if schooled this way' is a second, looser hint at the adjective learned.
explanation.definitionFit: To have heard about something is to have learned of it, a straightforward synonym in the past tense.

clue.text: An old-fashioned challenge–though it might be a selling point that has to bring things home to you.

parts.note: a stand is a stall from which goods are sold
and joins the two parts, as the clue's has to adds one thing to another
to deliver is to bring goods to your door

explanation.surface: An outdated demand is likened to a market stall that brings purchases to your house.
explanation.walkthrough: Stand and deliver! was the highwayman's command to coach travellers: stop and hand over your valuables.
explanation.definitionFit: The highwayman's cry is a challenge from a bygone era of robbery on the open road.

clue.text: Sometimes associated with drabs.

parts.note: the word paired with drabs in the set phrase meaning small irregular amounts

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is dribs and drabs, meaning in small scattered quantities.
explanation.definitionFit: Dribs are small amounts, found almost only in the idiom pairing them with drabs.

clue.text: See 24
In Oklahoma it is all right to get a sort of lust with a final part.

definitions.note: the answer is a city in Oklahoma, not a phrase meaning in Oklahoma

indicators.note: a sort of lust is a version of the word lust with its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Oklahomans are said to approve of a kind of desire, given a suitable ending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' rearranges LUST into TULS, and A is added as the final part.
explanation.definitionFit: Tulsa is the second-largest city in the state of Oklahoma, so it lies in that state.

clue.text: Stir the broth, just for a heartbeat.

indicators.note: stirring the broth mixes it up, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Give the soup a quick stir, it only takes a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: A throb is a strong pulse, the beating felt from the heart.

clue.text: Does it provide oxygen or just a trip?

definitions.text: Does it provide oxygen or just a trip?

parts.words: Does it provide oxygen or just a trip?
parts.note: one sense is a pipe carrying air to a diver; the other is a company selling flights

explanation.walkthrough: An air line is a hose that feeds air to a diver or a mask; an airline is a carrier that just flies you somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both an air-supply hose and a company operating passenger flights.

clue.text: An ordinary form of transportation with a slightly bigger version–or even one you can sleep in.

parts.note: the everyday motor car
a van is a somewhat larger vehicle than a car

explanation.surface: Climbing the ladder of vehicles from car to van to one with beds.
explanation.walkthrough: A caravan is a towed holiday home with beds, what Americans call a camper trailer.
explanation.definitionFit: A caravan is a vehicle fitted out for living, with beds so travellers can stay overnight.

clue.text: Phonemes I speak secretly may spell one's downfall.

indicators.note: the answer is tucked away secretly across the words phonemes I speak

parts.note: the answer's letters run across the end of phonemes, the word I and the start of speak

explanation.surface: Whispered speech sounds might spell the ruin of the speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: A nemesis is the agent of someone's ruin, named after the Greek goddess of retribution.

clue.text: Worked hard in the spot where one might find a scientist, with nothing to color.

parts.words: the spot where one might find a scientist
parts.note: a scientist works in a lab
O is the round figure zero
red is a color

explanation.surface: A scientist toiled in the lab, with nothing to paint with.
explanation.walkthrough: The spelling is American: LABORED, not British LABOURED.
explanation.definitionFit: To labor is to toil, so labored is the past tense of working hard.
